clue.text: Respectable Windsor woman sees smart pig discomfited

indicators.note: discomfited means thrown into disorder, so the letters of these words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A proper lady of Windsor watches a clever pig being put out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discomfited' rearranges SEES SMART PIG. The definition points to one of Shakespeare's Merry Wives of Windsor, the honest wife Falstaff tries to seduce.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Merry Wives of Windsor she is the virtuous wife who outwits Falstaff, a respectable townswoman of Windsor.

clue.text: Grace Aguilar's courtier Ferdinand sees Spain cocooned in ethics

indicators.note: cocooned in means wrapped inside, so the Spain letter sits within the ethics word

parts.note: E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: A Spanish courtier in a novel finds his country wrapped up in moral questions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cocooned in' puts E inside MORALS. Grace Aguilar's novel The Vale of Cedars features the Spanish courtier Ferdinand Morales.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferdinand Morales is a character in Grace Aguilar's historical romance The Vale of Cedars, set at the Spanish court.

clue.text: She crewed with Charlie Allnut in Africa

definitions.text: She crewed with Charlie Allnut in Africa

parts.words: She crewed with Charlie Allnut in Africa
parts.note: C. S. Forester's novel The African Queen has a missionary's sister travel downriver on Allnut's boat

explanation.surface: A woman joins a riverboat captain as crew in Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose is the prim spinster heroine of The African Queen, Allnut's only shipmate on the launch.

clue.text: Unwilling, like E.R. Braithwaite's neighbours

explanation.surface: An author's neighbours seem not to want to cooperate.
explanation.walkthrough: E. R. Braithwaite's 1972 memoir of race relations in Britain is called Reluctant Neighbours.
explanation.definitionFit: Unwilling means grudging or loath; Braithwaite, author of To Sir, With Love, also wrote a book titled after such neighbours.

clue.text: What's become of Waring Since he gave us all the (? Browning)

definitions.text: What's become of Waring Since he gave us all the

parts.words: What's become of Waring Since he gave us all the
parts.note: the opening lines of Browning's poem Waring, with the final word of the second line missing

explanation.surface: A line of Browning's verse breaks off just before its last word.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's Waring opens: 'What's become of Waring / Since he gave us all the slip?' The solver supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone the slip is an idiom for escaping them unnoticed, as Waring did his friends.

clue.text: Tie chaps in a knot with style imitation

indicators.note: tied in a knot means twisted up, so the letters of these words are tangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Some men are told to tie their neckwear stylishly in imitation of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a knot' rearranges TIE CHAPS; 'with' just joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A work that copies another artist's manner is a deliberate imitation of that style.

clue.text: Some dish Galahad was pursuing

explanation.surface: A knight goes after a particular plate.
explanation.definitionFit: The holy vessel of Arthurian legend was a dish or cup, and Sir Galahad is the knight who achieved its quest.

clue.text: Conspirator lit up in undisciplined ship

indicators.note: in means the reversed word is placed inside the ship's name

parts.note: the USS Caine of Herman Wouk's The Caine Mutiny, a ship whose crew mutinied

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards

explanation.surface: A plotter sets things alight aboard a rebellious vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reads the word backwards, as a down clue runs; 'undisciplined ship' is Herman Wouk's mutinous USS Caine. Catiline plotted against the Roman Republic and was denounced by Cicero.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucius Sergius Catilina led the plot to overthrow the Roman Republic in 63 BC.

clue.text: Two such in Le Carré book, possibly allowed by one 12 at

annotationWithheld.why: Two such in Le Carré book, possibly allowed by one 12 at (6): the clue ends on 'at', so the fielding position (probably a cross-reference) is cut off
annotationWithheld.clue: Two such in Le Carré book, possibly allowed by one 12 at

clue.text: Ruler's accessories may accrue to author

explanation.surface: A king's neckwear and an author's earnings are set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal ties would be a monarch's neckwear; payments to a writer per copy sold are the usual sense.

clue.text: Instrument makers from Birmingham (at Italian rates)

indicators.note: from means the letters are taken out of a run of the following words

explanation.surface: Violin makers are said to come from Birmingham, charging Italian prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points to letters inside BirminghAM AT Italian; 'rates' only completes the surface. The Amati family made violins in Cremona.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amati were a Cremonese family of violin makers, teachers of Stradivari.

clue.text: Cyril's dreadful poems

indicators.note: dreadful suggests a mess, so the letters of the name are scrambled

parts.note: the name with its possessive S, used as letters

explanation.surface: Cyril has written some terrible verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadful' rearranges CYRILS, the S of the possessive included.
explanation.definitionFit: Short poems, especially songs or verse expressing feeling, are called by this word.

clue.text: Novelist eponymously associated with poet by Simon Raven

definitions.text: eponymously associated with poet by Simon Raven

explanation.surface: A novelist is linked by name to a poet in another writer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Raven's novel Fielding Gray takes its title character's name from two writers.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry is the author of Tom Jones; Simon Raven named his character Fielding Gray, joining that novelist's surname to the poet Thomas Gray's.

clue.text: Said of breakfast food regularly produced by Dickens

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the word for breakfast food is taken by its sound

parts.note: cornflakes and porridge are breakfast cereals

explanation.surface: Dickens produces breakfast food at regular intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens published most of his novels in monthly or weekly instalments.
explanation.definitionFit: A story issued in instalments appears regularly, as Dickens's novels did in magazines.

clue.text: His English was basic, and his criticism practical

definitions.text: His English was basic, and his criticism practical

parts.words: His English was basic, and his criticism practical
parts.note: names two works of the Cambridge critic I. A.: Basic English and Practical Criticism

explanation.surface: A man's English was elementary but his critiques sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: I. A. Richards promoted Basic English, an 850-word simplified language, and wrote Practical Criticism (1929).
explanation.definitionFit: The critic I. A. Richards is known for championing Basic English and for his book Practical Criticism.

clue.text: Lawrence poem, part of the Great Hebridean cycle

indicators.note: part of means the letters are a stretch running across the following words

explanation.surface: A Lawrence poem is said to belong to a Scottish island cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of' points to greaT HEBRIDEan. D. H. Lawrence wrote a poem of that name about his dead mother.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence's poem of this title describes his mother lying dead, looking young like a bride.

clue.text: Ten support Belgian province to produce Venetian senator

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece stands below the other

parts.note: Brabant is a region of Belgium
10 written in letters that look like the digits

explanation.surface: Ten people prop up a Belgian region to create a senator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support' places IO beneath BRABANT. Brabantio is Desdemona's father in Othello.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Othello, Desdemona's father is a senator of Venice.

clue.text: Psalm found on church stool 51

explanation.surface: A psalm is discovered on a church seat numbered 51.
explanation.walkthrough: Psalm 51 opens 'Miserere mei'; the word is also another name for a misericord, the ledge under a hinged choir seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Psalm 51 is known by its Latin opening; a misericord, the ledge on a choir stall seat, is also called by this name.

clue.text: Poet's party

parts.note: a gathering that gives the title to a T. S. Eliot verse play, named for the drink served

explanation.surface: A poet throws a party.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot's verse drama is The Cocktail Party, a kind of drinks gathering.

clue.text: Constructor (from Thrace) of Alexander's Bridge

indicators.note: from here means formed out of, so the letters of the place are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone from ancient Thrace built a bridge for Alexander.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' rearranges THRACE. Alexander's Bridge (1912) was Willa Cather's first novel, about a bridge engineer.
explanation.definitionFit: Willa Cather wrote the novel Alexander's Bridge, so as author she built it.

clue.text: Those of Babylon are found in Arden

explanation.surface: Babylon's rivers turn up in the Forest of Arden.
explanation.walkthrough: Psalm 137 begins 'By the waters of Babylon'. Arden is Elizabeth Arden, the cosmetics firm that sells toilet waters, not Shakespeare's forest.
explanation.definitionFit: Psalm 137 mourns by the rivers of Babylon; scented toilet lotions are sold by a cosmetics house.

clue.text: "The swarthy —, with wares from Spain and Afric" (Bulwer- Lytton, Harold)

definitions.text: The swarthy —, with wares from Spain and Afric

parts.words: The swarthy —, with wares from Spain and Afric
parts.note: a line from Bulwer-Lytton's poem Harold with the noun for a Moorish trader left out

explanation.surface: A quotation from Bulwer-Lytton about a dark-skinned merchant with goods from Spain and Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval Europeans used this word for an Arab or Muslim, fitting a trader from Moorish Spain and North Africa.

clue.text: Conveyance of New York island arranged by Dos Passos

definitions.text: of New York island arranged by Dos Passos

explanation.surface: A transport deal over a New York island is set up by a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: John Dos Passos wrote the novel Manhattan Transfer (1925); Manhattan is the New York island.
explanation.definitionFit: Conveyance is the legal passing of property to another owner; Dos Passos set it beside Manhattan for his novel's title.

clue.text: Part of character in Moliere's The Miser, if analysed

indicators.note: in means the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Analysing The Miser reveals part of a Molière character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to miSER IF. 'Character' means a printed letter, not a person in a play.
explanation.definitionFit: A serif is the small stroke finishing a typeface letter's stem, part of a printed letter.

clue.text: Blake thought that the strongest poison came from his laurel crown

definitions.text: Blake thought that the strongest poison came from his laurel crown

parts.words: Blake thought that the strongest poison came from his laurel crown
parts.note: Blake's couplet 'The strongest poison ever known / Came from ...'s laurel crown', naming the Roman wearer

explanation.surface: Blake declares a ruler's laurel wreath the deadliest poison.
explanation.definitionFit: In Blake's Auguries of Innocence the laurel crown of the Roman dictator stands for imperial power's poison.

clue.text: Reported which town?

parts.note: heard aloud the question asks about a witch town, the Massachusetts place of the 1692 trials

explanation.surface: Someone asks which town was mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, 'which' sounds like 'witch'. The Salem witch trials of 1692 are the subject of Arthur Miller's The Crucible.
explanation.definitionFit: The Massachusetts town is famous for its witch trials of 1692.

clue.text: Bennett gave him his share (he had his pride, no doubt)

definitions.text: he had his pride, no doubt

explanation.surface: A writer gave someone a share, and that someone was proud.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnold Bennett wrote the novel The Lion's Share (1916). A group of the big cats is called a pride.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Bennett titled a novel after the big cat's share; that cat lives in a group called a pride.

clue.text: Ivy Compton-Burnett implied he should be better

definitions.text: Ivy Compton-Burnett implied he should be better

parts.words: Ivy Compton-Burnett implied he should be better
parts.note: her novel ... and Betters pairs the senior person with the superior one

explanation.surface: A novelist suggested that a man ought to improve.
explanation.walkthrough: Ivy Compton-Burnett's 1944 novel is Elders and Betters, coupling the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: An older person, in the phrase 'elders and betters', is assumed to be one's superior.

clue.text: Form mastered by Richardson: his characters corresponded so well

definitions.text: Form mastered by Richardson: his characters corresponded so well

parts.words: Form mastered by Richardson: his characters corresponded so well
parts.note: Samuel Richardson's Pamela and Clarissa are told entirely through letters the characters write

explanation.surface: Richardson's characters exchanged letters with great skill.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Richardson's novels Pamela and Clarissa are told in letters; 'corresponded' means wrote letters, not matched.
explanation.definitionFit: A novel in the form of letters is written in the letter-writing manner, Richardson's speciality.

clue.text: Powell characters not found in the morning room

definitions.text: not found in the morning room

explanation.surface: Some of Powell's characters are absent from the morning room.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Powell's first novel was Afternoon Men (1931); people found later in the day would not be in a morning room.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Powell's first novel is titled after its idle socialites; men of the later part of the day are absent before noon.
